title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of recognizing and releasing our attachments to suffering, which arises from our mistaken perception of a separate self. By letting go of these attachments and cultivating mindfulness and wisdom, we can break free from the cycle of suffering and find ease in life. This involves understanding that our thoughts and perceptions are not reality, but rather a way of experiencing it, and learning to respond to life's complexities with greater freedom and liberation.

sentences.text: Good evening, and welcome to the Four Noble Truths, Part 2.
If you were here last week, I hope you had an opportunity to investigate for yourself the truth of suffering, because it is a very personal investigation.
In Part 2, we will be doing a little bit less talking from my side, and we will have a small group discussion towards the end.
We won't need much time to talk about this, actually.
The teaching is very simple.
It is the practice of the teaching that trips us up.
So to say what the Four Noble Truths are takes very little time, and doing it is the rest of our lives.
Now I'm going to do cliff notes on the First Noble Truth, the truth of suffering, that we talked about last week.
This is the truth that birth, sickness, old age, death, change, and circumstance in general involve suffering.
This is ease, unease, physical and mental pain in obvious and very subtle forms.
We almost always feel an undercurrent of anxiety and uncertainty.
For tonight's talk, I leaned on the book The Truth of Suffering by Chokyam Trungpa Rinpoche.
So we will be investigating the truth of the cause of suffering and the truth of the end of suffering.
To avoid getting lost in details, let us first look at the big picture.
The cause of our suffering stems from craving and fundamental ignorance.
We suffer because of our mistaken belief that we are a separate, independent self, a solid I.
The painful and futile structure to maintain this delusion of ego is known as samsara, or cyclic existence.
So let's look at life.
Maybe we can observe that our attachments are less to things.
Our attachment is more to our plans that we have for all those things out there.
Also, please do not use this teaching to beat yourself up.
We make mistakes all the time.
We cannot avoid it.
So if we think this will fix all our mistakes, I'm sorry.
The key is to use the knowledge we have to work on preventing future mistakes and knowing that they will continue to happen.
The end of suffering can come through choosing to follow the path out of suffering.
By living ethically, practicing meditation, and developing wisdom, we can exactly take the same journey to enlightenment and freedom from suffering that the Buddhas take.
Suffering can end because our awakened mind can always be available to us.
When craving and clinging cease or are confined, we end our suffering.
So what is the suffering we want to end?
Please note, the Buddha did not say life is suffering.
He defined suffering, which is dukkha in the Pali language.
He said:
*Birth is dukkha, aging is dukkha, illness is dukkha, death is dukkha, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are dukkha.
Association with the unbeloved is dukkha.
Separation from the loved is dukkha.
Not getting what is wanted is dukkha.*
So now, onward to a more detailed look at the cause of suffering.
The short explanation of the cause of suffering is this.
In ignorance, we have a thirst, a desire, craving, or clinging to impermanent states and things.
This clinging and craving produces results or consequences, which lead to more of the same.
This is also known as karma.
The plain translation of karma is actually consequence or action.
If you would like to study this more deeply, you can take a look at dependent origination, or the chain of causation.
This craving leads to renewed becoming, staying in my rut, keeping me trapped to repeat old mistakes over and over and over, in rebirth and renewed dissatisfaction.
So I added rebirth.
It is a basic Buddhist teaching, but please don't ask me any questions about it.
I have no experience with it, at least not as far as I remember.
It is a key Buddhist teaching though, and yet my Zen practice keeps me on the straight and narrow.
I'm not going to talk theory.
I don't know anything about rebirth.

So craving includes the following types of craving: craving for sense pleasures, craving to continue the cycle of life and death, including rebirth, and craving to not experience reality and painful feelings.
Craving and suffering actually give rise to each other.
They are interdependent and they come into existence together.
We suffer and we want to end our suffering, so we crave for a world that is different, and then we get into distractions and seeking pleasure and avoiding pain.
Often that starts with a very small thought, with a very small feeling right here, and if we can catch it at that moment, we actually have a pretty good chance of stopping it.
Often we are not aware of that tender feeling, that slight minor thought, and so it takes on a life of its own.
And the more time we spend with it, the bigger it gets.
It's like when a train starts moving, it's very easy to stop, but when it's blasting full speed, it takes half a mile.
So here's a personal example.
For many years, I had this dream of hiking through the Torres in Chile once I retired.
I loved that place, the clear air and the wind, the beauty and the hostility of the terrain, the cold, the way it made me feel.
I knew where I wanted to go, what I wanted to see, and I knew exactly how it was going to be.
I spent quite a time dreaming about it over 25 years, but when retirement came about, it did not happen.
My knee cannot take the uneven ground and weight of a loaded backpack.
I am 25 years older than the origin of this dream.
I may still go on this hike, who knows, but it will be very different from my original dream.
If I insist on this original dream, I will suffer.
I will complain to myself, and you can be pretty sure that everybody around me is going to suffer.
I will inflict physical suffering on myself.
I will be angry and dissatisfied, and I will therefore create more suffering.
With all this craving and clinging, with taking everything personal, we don't behave that well.
We expect happiness from states and things which are impermanent and which we do not control, and therefore we cannot attain real happiness through that method.
I will get old, I hope, and I will get sick.
I look into the mirror where an old woman is laughing at me and my thought, "But it's finally time to get the bikini body after all."
So let's face it, my thinking is off, and the next minute the world is against me, and I need to blame somebody or something if I do not watch my mind.
So what is the alternative?
The alternative is the end of suffering.
So how can I get in touch with how this suffering arises?
I'm going to speak just for myself now because all this is extremely personal and individual.
I confess my ignorance.
I see that I rather relate with that which I like, and that I try to avoid that which is unpleasant.
Sometimes we feel like an unhealthy mental growth, but dealing with it and removing it is just very painful, and so I'd rather stay in my rut.
That's where the eightfold noble path comes in.
It points a way out of the rut.
The excellence of the Buddha's teaching lies in this: it is simple and it is workable.
It requires, however, that first we understand dukkha, suffering, and not somebody else's suffering, but our own.
We need to see that attachments and clinging create and continue suffering.
Here is the good news.

Through practicing the path, we can end dukkha, our suffering, and the eightfold path is this: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
The way out of our rut and to perceive reality, what is going on, lies in mindfulness and in zazen.
In zazen, we detach from our ego and our ego-driven worldview.
We see ourselves and our actions with more space.
In this space, we find the room to review our actions and maybe to take different actions and to make decisions.
So we need to operate through knee-jerk reactions.
We need to stop that.
We stay with what we do in reality and not in delusion.
In other words, let's wake up to what is around us.
Practicing the Four Noble Truth is not probably instant enlightenment, but I can guarantee that its practice will bring ease into our life and in the life of the people around us.
The truth and the eightfold path are very simple and easy to understand.
However, they are hard to practice.
Being mindful of what I do and say and my intentions and aspirations, to see the arising of delusion, we will make mistakes.
We hurt people.
We get lost in entertainment and distraction.
However, I need to face what I did and how it happened.
If I hurt someone, if I made a mistake, if I get lost, I look at what happened and how it happened and I start again, over and over.
The universe does not change because I think reality is inconvenient.
The one thing I can change is my response to reality.
I can stop trying to impose the laws of reality that I create in my head: if I do A, B must happen.
Instead of B, which would happen if the world would function as I think, I might get L through W.
This does not mean there is something wrong with the world.
There is nothing wrong with reality.
It means that my thought model is incorrect and it will always be incorrect and that this world is way more complicated than my thought model.
The truth of the end of suffering is personal.
It is not magic or only available to some special people.
It is our birthright and has been that from the beginning of time.
It does not mean there is no pain.
If you break a bone, it hurts.
I continue to grow older.
A person I love dies.
There is pain.
This is all part of being a living person.
Taking it personal, blaming others and complaining are samsara games.
Samsara is the cycle of birth and death that arises from grasping and fixation on experiences and the permanent self.
Samsara arises out of ignorance and it is characterized by pleasure and aversion.
Samsara is the world of suffering.
The escape hatch from samsara is working on my conduct and seeing the world through practicing the eightfold path.
To quote Chokyam Trungpa Rinpoche:
*The experience of cessation is very personal and real, like the practice of meditation.
Generally, however, our experiences of freedom or liberation are quite sparse and mute.
And when we do have the occasional glimpse of freedom, we try to catch it, so we lose it.
But it is possible to extend such glimpses.*
End quote.
I want to end here and leave some room for a small group discussion.
So let us do dyads.
Please find a partner and let's try to space out a little.
And once you've found a space, I will ring a bell.
Each person will have five minutes.
While the other person speaks, please pay attention with all you got.
Let it flow and don't try to formulate your arguments or your response while the other person is speaking.
If the other person stops speaking before the time is up, please listen to the silence.
When I ring the bell, please finish your sentence and let the other person have their turn.
When the third bell rings, please come back to your seat.
And also, please treat what you hear with respect and confidentiality.
And the theme is whatever comes up for you around the practice of the Four Noble Truths, either what you have practiced before or what we talked about tonight.
So thank you very much.
